title: Absolute or relative path?
description: Decide whether each path is absolute or relative.

items.why: It starts with `/`, so it describes the way from the root and means the same file wherever you are.
It does not start with `/`. `..` means the parent of the current directory, so the result depends on where you are.
It looks relative, but the shell replaces `~` with the home directory before the command runs. The command sees `/home/mira/notes.txt`, which starts with `/`.
`.` means the current directory, so this path starts from where you are.
A single dot is the current directory, which is relative by definition.
It does not start with `/`, so it is found starting from the current directory.
The root directory itself starts with `/`, so it is an absolute path.
It starts at the root, so it points to the same directory from anywhere.
Two dots mean "one level up from here", which depends on the current directory.
The first character is not `/`, so this is a path below the current directory. It only works if `etc` is there.
It starts with `/`, so it is the same place from every directory.
Without the leading `/` it is read from the current directory: `/home/mira/projects/website` when Mira is in her home.
The shell turns `~jonas` into Jonas’s home, so the command gets `/home/jonas/art`, an absolute path.
The trailing slash only says it is a directory. It does not start with `/`, so it is relative.
